The five special members are the functions that create, copy, move and destroy an object of a class: the destructor, the copy constructor, the copy assignment operator, the move constructor and the move assignment operator. Declaring any one of them yourself changes what the compiler still generates for the rest, so Core Guidelines C.21 asks you to declare all five together, the moves included, even when some are only

The problem shows up in a class that owns a resource through a raw handle, a pointer to a heap array it allocated itself. With only a destructor declared, the compiler still generates a copy constructor that copies the pointer, so two objects own one array, and both destructors free it: a double free. The same destructor also removes the compiler's move constructor and move assignment, so an rvalue falls back to copying instead of moving, or to a deleted operation if copying was disabled.

The mechanism is one job per member. The destructor frees the array once. The copy constructor allocates an array of its own and copies the values into it, so the copy can change without touching the original. The moves take the pointer and the size with
, leaving the source empty, and they are
because moving a pointer and an integer cannot fail. Copy assignment is written as copy-and-swap: it builds the complete copy first, the only step that can throw, then swaps it into
with operations that cannot throw, which gives the strong exception guarantee and survives self-assignment without a test for it.
What it costs is writing and testing five functions correctly, for every class that does this. When every member already manages itself, a

copies deeply, moves without throwing, and survives self-assignment on its own, so the compiler's member-wise versions are already correct, and hand-written ones only add code that can go wrong. That is the Rule of Zero: hold resources through members that already behave, and declare none of the five yourself.
You meet this split in the robot's own classes: the rare one that wraps a raw resource directly writes all five, and everything that instead holds a
gets them for free. The interview question's second half is exactly this choice, why the answer with zero declared members is the better one whenever you can reach it.

c.v: builds each new element in place, so every count in the first three lines comes from growth. GCC 13's vector doubles its capacity, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and relocates 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements on the way. With a move that isn't

, all 31 become copies, and for a type that owns memory each copy is an allocation. Nothing warns: the program is correct and slower. O'Dwyer's post on the vector pessimisation walks through the same case, and Core Guidelines

moves for this reason. The third line is the exception. A move-only type has no copy to fall back on, so the vector moves it anyway and gives up the strong guarantee: if one of those moves threw, the effects would be unspecified.
